analysis.one_liner: Raises tax penalties on corporations using offshore tax havens and favors federal contractors that keep jobs in the U.S.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2010, referred to two House committees, and never received a vote before Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Treasury Department to publish a list of countries that function as corporate tax havens, then sharply increased tax penalties on corporations whose tax underpayments or fraud involved money in those countries. It also would have given a preference in federal contract awards to companies that had not laid off a U.S. worker and moved the same job overseas, with fines and a two-year contracting ban for false answers. New revenue was set aside for reducing the federal debt.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. workers whose jobs would be harder to move offshore, because federal contractors that outsource would lose contract preferences, and honest taxpayers who now effectively subsidize corporations that shift profits to tax havens.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have directed Treasury to publish and update every three years a list of corporate tax haven countries, judged by criteria such as low tax rates, lack of information sharing, and lack of transparency.

It would have raised corporate penalties for tax underpayments, reportable-transaction understatements, and fraud involving tax haven countries — for example, tripling the accuracy-related penalty from 20% to 60% and doubling criminal fine maximums from $500,000 to $1,000,000.

It would have given a preference in federal contracts to companies that had not engaged in outsourcing, defined as laying off a U.S. worker and hiring someone overseas to do the same job, and imposed civil penalties up to the contract's value plus a two-year debarment for false statements.
Revenue generated by the bill was set aside for reducing the public debt.

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations using tax haven countries to underpay taxes, and companies that lay off U.S. workers and move those jobs abroad while seeking or holding federal contracts.
analysis.who_pays_short: Tax-haven users and outsourcing federal contractors

drawbacks.text: Business groups would argue that tripling penalties and branding countries as tax havens by unilateral U.S. determination could raise compliance costs and invite disputes with other countries and multinational firms operating lawfully abroad.

The outsourcing preference is narrow and arguably easy to work around: it applies only to the specific act of laying off a U.S. worker and moving that same job abroad, not to broader profit-shifting or hiring abroad without a domestic layoff, so the practical job-protection effect may be modest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core is stronger enforcement against corporate tax avoidance and a modest penalty for offshoring federal contract work. The costs fall on firms whose behavior the bill targets, and the main honest concern is design: the outsourcing definition is narrow and a unilateral tax haven list could create friction. On balance the benefits to workers and honest taxpayers outweigh these costs, but the measure never advanced far enough for those trade-offs to be tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means and Oversight and Government Reform committees and neither one ever took it up, so it died when that Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry McNerney introduced the bill on June 29, 2010, with Reps. Bishop of New York and Peters as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the Ways and Means Committee and the Oversight and Government Reform Committee for consideration of provisions within their jurisdiction.
The committees took no further action on the bill, and it received no vote in the House or Senate before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations using tax haven countries and federal contractors that outsource U.S. jobs are better off, because the higher penalties and contracting preferences were never enacted.

for.name: Reps. Tim Bishop and Gary Peters
for.role: Original cosponsors, U.S. House of Representatives
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; two additional Democratic members later cosponsored, for 2 cosponsors total.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for the tax penalty provisions and took no action, never holding a markup or vote.

against.name: House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral for the contracting provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral for the contracting preference provisions and took no action.

sides.party_line_note: All three House sponsors and both cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported the bill, and with only 2 cosponsors of 253 House Democrats, it drew minimal support even within the majority party.

industries.industry: Multinational corporations using offshore tax havens
industries.note: The bill would have tripled or doubled civil and criminal penalties for tax underpayments and fraud involving tax haven countries, directly raising the cost of shifting profits offshore. Blocking the bill preserves that channel of untaxed profit.

industries.industry: Federal contractors that outsource U.S. jobs
industries.note: Companies that lay off a U.S. worker and move the same job abroad would have lost preference in federal contract awards and faced fines up to the contract's value and a two-year debarment for false statements. The bill's death leaves those companies free to compete for federal work regardless of offshoring.

industries.industry: Onshore federal contractors and U.S.-based workers
industries.note: Firms keeping jobs in the United States would have gained a bidding edge for federal contracts, and the workers whose jobs are at risk of offshoring are the intended beneficiaries. The bill died before this preference ever took effect.
